title: The body as it is
hookLine: walking, standing, sitting, lying down: a poem that looks at the body plainly

cards: Some days you catch yourself in a shop window and think: not bad. Other days the bathroom mirror at seven in the morning says something else entirely.
Plenty of people swing between those two, pride and dislike, about the same body, sometimes within the same hour. Phones add filters to fix one side; ads sell the other.
The eleventh poem of the Sutta Nipata asks for something rarer than either. Not a better body, not a worse opinion of it. Just a clear look.

teach.b: The poem starts with movement. Walking or standing, sitting or lying down, bending and stretching: that's what a body does. Then it looks inside, the way an honest anatomy lesson would.
Bones and sinews, wrapped in skin and flesh. A belly, a liver, a heart, lungs, kidneys. Things the skin covers, so they aren't seen as they are.

Then it looks at what comes out: tears, sweat, the things that leave the body every day. Some listeners find this part uncomfortable, and that's worth noticing. The poem isn't trying to make anyone ashamed.

Its last lines name the point. Whoever thinks highly of themselves because of a body like this, or looks down on someone else because of theirs, what is that, the poem asks, except not seeing? So it cuts two ways at once.
Against vanity: this body is not a trophy.
Against contempt: no one is lesser because of theirs. What's left is steady and kind: a body that walks and bends and breathes, seen plainly.

teach.h: A WEEK OF LOOKING PAST THE SURFACE
teach.b: This week was about seeing plainly, too. Four kinds of seekers, and a robe that proves nothing. A slow slide, told cause by cause.
Not by birth, by deeds. The kindness poem, whole. Two spirits checking character.
A threat answered with calm. Each time, the poem looks past the surface, a robe, a birth, a threat, to what is actually there.

how: Contemplating the parts of the body is a traditional Buddhist meditation, taught especially to monastics; teachers present it as a way to loosen vanity and craving, not to cultivate disgust.

o: the body, seen plainly as it is
a sin committed with the body
the soul that lives inside the body

games.q: the body poem: tap the pairs.
p: the poem calls it not seeing

s: the poem's aim is to make people ashamed of their bodies
its last lines are against both vanity and contempt for others; the aim is seeing plainly.
the poem begins with the body's movements
walking, standing, sitting, lying down, bending and stretching.
the poem also warns against looking down on someone else's body
pride in one's own and contempt for another's are both called not seeing.

games.q: you've just looked at the body plainly, as the poem does. what does the poem say is the mistake to avoid?
o: feeling anything at all about your body.
pride in your own body or contempt for someone else's.
games.why: the last verse names both: thinking highly of yourself, or looking down on another, because of a body. that's not seeing.

practice: Feel your feet, your hands, the weight in the chair, the breath moving the belly, and somewhere inside, a heart working without asking for thanks.
If a judgment comes, too heavy, too tired, not bad, name it, judging, and come back to the plain feeling: warm here, tight there, moving, breathing, a body as it is.

wordCard.voice: Kaya, the body, in Pali. The Sutta Nipata's eleventh poem: seeing the body plainly, so there's no ground for pride in your own or contempt for anyone else's. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali kaya: body. Sn 1.11 is sometimes called the Kayavicchandanika Sutta, on turning away from desire for the body.

carryVoice: Your line: as it is. No trophy, and nothing to look down on. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 10 / Digha Nikaya 22: contemplation of the parts of the body
